prompt: Two ways to deliver the same 60-finding audit to a client. **A:** a PDF report and a slide deck, emailed to the head of product, with a thank-you reply the next day. **B:** the same findings entered as individual tickets in the client's own tracker, each with a suggested owning team and a rough size estimate, presented in the same meeting. Six months later, which is more likely to have produced actual fixes, and why?

options.text: A — a polished PDF and slide deck signal seriousness and are more likely to be taken up by leadership
B — the findings are already inside the system the team uses to decide what to work on, instead of needing someone to manually move them there later
Neither — what matters is whether the client's culture values accessibility, not how the findings were delivered
A — findings that stay outside the tracker get more attention precisely because they don't get lost among routine tickets

hints: Ask which version a busy engineering manager, three weeks later, would actually see without anyone reminding them.
The tracker is the system sprint planning actually reads from. A PDF is not.
explanation: B. A polished PDF can absolutely signal seriousness in the room — and still be invisible to the tracker three weeks later, when the meeting is a memory and sprint planning runs entirely off the board. Findings already sitting as tickets, in the same board the team plans real work from, survive that gap by default; findings sitting in an inbox or a shared drive require someone to remember them, find time, and manually re-enter them, which is exactly the step that most often never happens. Client culture matters too, but it's a separate variable — this choice changes the odds regardless of how the culture leans.

prompt: You've just delivered an audit as a PDF and a slide deck — the client's process, not yours, and you couldn't change it this time. Before you consider the engagement finished, write the two- or three-sentence follow-up message you'd send that gives the findings the best chance of surviving contact with the client's actual backlog. Assume you cannot personally file tickets in their tracker.
hints: You can't file the tickets, but you can ask for something small, specific and sayable-yes-to.
A date beats a general request. 'Could someone triage the top ten by Friday' is answerable; 'please prioritise this' is not.
explanation: A strong message names a small number of the highest-severity findings specifically (not all 60), asks a named or role-addressed person to move just those into the tracker, and proposes a concrete date for that to happen — for example: "Could someone on the checkout team move the five Blocker-severity findings (#3, #7, #12, #19, #24) into your board this week, even without owners assigned yet? Happy to join a fifteen-minute call if that's faster than reading through them again." This is answerable in a way "please make sure this gets actioned" is not — it names a person-shaped task, a small scope, and a date, which is the whole difference this lesson is about.

prompt: Which of these is the clearest real signal of accountability, versus something that only resembles it?

options.text: An annual all-staff accessibility awareness training with a 100% completion rate
A named role whose quarterly goals include a specific remediation target, with sprint capacity reserved to hit it
A public accessibility statement committing to 'continuous improvement'
A dedicated internal Slack channel where accessibility questions get answered

hints: Ask what changes for one specific person's job if the work doesn't happen this quarter.
Training, statements and channels can all exist alongside zero accountability, and often do.
explanation: Only the named role with a measurable goal and reserved capacity has a mechanism that makes non-delivery visible and attributable to someone. Training raises awareness but doesn't survive contact with a busy quarter; a public statement commits the company in the abstract but names no individual; a channel provides a place to ask, not a guarantee anyone with authority answers or acts. The tell, in all three wrong answers, is the same: nothing about any specific person's job changes if the work doesn't happen.

prompt: True or false: assigning accessibility as "everyone's responsibility" in a handbook is, in practice, functionally similar to assigning it to nobody.

config.statement: Assigning accessibility as "everyone's responsibility" in a company handbook is functionally similar to assigning it to nobody.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and explains the mechanism — that a task with no named owner, budget or review criteria has no individual whose job is affected by whether it happens — not just that the statement 'sounds vague.'

hints: Ask what happens to one specific person's workload or performance review if the task doesn't get done this quarter.
The statement can be completely sincere and still fail as a mechanism.
explanation: True. The sincerity of the statement isn't the issue — the mechanism is. When a task belongs to everyone equally, it belongs, in the sense that matters for whether it actually happens, to no one: nobody's calendar has protected time for it, nobody's performance review reflects whether it happened, and whoever is busiest that quarter can deprioritise it without any individual accountability. Real ownership requires a name attached to a specific, measurable piece of the work, with time or budget set aside to do it.

prompt: A remediation programme is struggling to get fixes scheduled. Someone proposes keeping the master spreadsheet for reporting, but also entering each fix as an ordinary ticket, sized in the team's normal story points, in the backlog of the team that owns the affected code. What is this change most likely to do?

options.text: Nothing — the total amount of work still has to compete for the same limited developer time either way

Increase the rate fixes actually get scheduled, because each one now competes ticket-by-ticket against similarly-sized work in a process that already runs every sprint, instead of as a whole programme against a rare, high-stakes competition
Make the fixes harder to track, since progress is no longer visible in one place
Only help if the team also hires dedicated accessibility engineers

hints: The total work is the same either way — what changes is how often, and against what, each individual piece competes for attention.
Nothing about this change requires new headcount.
explanation: The second option. Total developer time available doesn't change, but this isn't about total time — it's about how often each fix gets a fair shot at being picked, and against what. A quarterly steering-committee competition happens four times a year, against work with harder deadlines; ordinary sprint planning happens every one to two weeks, comparing tickets of similar size on the same terms. Keeping the spreadsheet for reporting solves the tracking-visibility problem the third answer raises without needing to sacrifice the scheduling improvement, and none of it requires new headcount.

prompt:
Rewrite this ticket so it's shaped the way a normal sprint planning process can actually evaluate and slot in:

"Accessibility issue #22: fix date picker per audit. See attached PDF page 14."

You don't have the original PDF — invent plausible, specific details (which control, what's wrong, what fixed looks like) consistent with a real date-picker accessibility finding.
hints: A workable ticket names the real component, gives a rough size estimate, and states acceptance criteria specific enough that someone could verify the fix without re-reading the original audit.
Acceptance criteria should describe an observable, testable outcome — not just 'accessible now'.
explanation: A strong rewrite might read: "Custom date picker on /checkout/delivery is a <div> grid with no roles or keyboard support — screen reader users cannot select a date and keyboard users cannot operate it at all. Fix: rebuild using native semantics or full ARIA grid pattern with keyboard support. Estimate: 5 points. Acceptance: NVDA and VoiceOver announce each date cell's role and state; full keyboard operation (arrow keys to move, Enter to select, Escape to close); axe DevTools passes with no date-picker violations. WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2." What makes this workable is exactly what the lesson named: a real component, a size estimate in the team's own units, and acceptance criteria specific enough to verify without anyone re-reading the original finding.

prompt: Sort each item by whether it's real evidence of accessibility work, or a sign of compliance theatre.

items.text: A VPAT with a test date, named tester, specific browser/AT combinations, and three honestly listed partial-conformance exceptions
A VPAT claiming full AA conformance across every criterion with no date, tester or methodology listed
An internal report showing which of last quarter's audit findings were fixed, retested, and confirmed with the original assistive technology
A purchased 'accessibility certified' seal with no report available on request
A public statement naming the specific WCAG version tested against, the date, and a named contact for reporting new issues

hints: Ask of each one: is there something specific and checkable behind this claim, or just the claim itself?
explanation: The pattern across all five: real evidence names who, when, against what, and — usually — what the honest limitations were. Theatre is a claim with nothing checkable behind it, however confident or official-looking the claim's packaging is. A seal or a statement can be perfectly genuine; the diagnostic is always whether a specific, checkable report exists behind it.

prompt: True or false: a VPAT claiming full conformance is, by itself, sufficient proof that a product has actually been remediated.

config.statement: A VPAT claiming full conformance is, by itself, sufficient proof that a product has actually been remediated.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names what would actually be needed alongside the VPAT — a test date, named tester, methodology or specific listed exceptions — not just that VPATs 'can be wrong.'

hints: A document can claim anything. The question is what would let someone check whether the claim is true.
What's missing from a VPAT with 'Supports' on every line and nothing else?
explanation: False. A VPAT is a self-declared claim, and self-declared claims are only as trustworthy as what's checkable behind them — a test date, a named tester, a stated methodology, and, for anything genuinely tested at real scale, some honestly listed exceptions. A VPAT with none of that attached is a claim shaped like evidence, not evidence itself, and treating it as sufficient proof is exactly the gap that lets compliance theatre pass as remediation.

prompt: Match each role to what they can actually authorise on their own, without anyone else's sign-off.

pairs.left: Engineering manager
pairs.right: Reshuffling their own team's next sprint, within existing headcount

pairs.left: In-house legal counsel
pairs.right: Requiring the company address a specific risk, and flagging exposure to leadership

pairs.left: VP of Product
pairs.right: Allocating roadmap capacity and budget for a multi-sprint effort

pairs.left: Individual contributor developer
pairs.right: Fixing something within a ticket already assigned to them

hints: Ask what changes immediately, with no further approval needed, if each person alone says yes.
explanation: Each role's real authority is narrower and more specific than their apparent seniority might suggest — an engineering manager can move their own team's next sprint but not add headcount or override a committed roadmap date; legal can create pressure and name risk but doesn't hold product budget; a VP of Product holds exactly the resource a multi-sprint effort needs. Matching the ask to the role that actually controls the resource is the whole point of this lesson.

prompt: Put these steps of finding and approaching the actual decision-maker in order.

items: Map the candidates: who is close to the work, who has formal authority, and who actually controls the specific resource needed
Identify which one holds the resource this specific ask requires — capacity, budget, or roadmap priority
Size the ask down to something small enough to fit inside one decision
Attach evidence scoped directly to that size, not a general case for accessibility
Ask for a yes or no by a specific date tied to a real event on their calendar

hints: Sizing the ask can't happen until you know whose resource you're asking for — that comes first.
explanation: Mapping and identifying the right person has to happen before sizing the ask, because what counts as 'small enough to be a decision' depends on what that specific person controls — a VP of Product's smallest decision is larger than an engineering manager's. Running this backwards, sizing an ask before knowing who it's for, is how proposals end up addressed to whoever's easiest to reach instead of whoever can actually say yes.

prompt: An audit was delivered as a 90-page PDF eight months ago. The engineering director says she 'definitely read it and it was good work.' None of the findings appear anywhere in the team's tracker. What's the blocker?

options.text: No routing — the findings never entered the system the team's actual sprint planning runs from
No ownership — nobody at the company is responsible for accessibility
Roadmap competition — the fixes lost out to higher-priority feature work

hints: There's no evidence yet that anyone was ever assigned to act on this, or that it was ever compared against other work at all.
explanation: No routing. The scenario doesn't yet show a competition being lost (roadmap competition) or an absence of anyone responsible in principle (ownership) — it shows a document that was read and liked, then never crossed the specific, mundane threshold of becoming tickets in the tool the team's real work runs through. That's the narrowest and most likely explanation given only what's described.

prompt: True or false: a company with a named "Head of Accessibility" title on the org chart necessarily has real ownership of accessibility work.

config.statement: A company with a named "Head of Accessibility" title on the org chart necessarily has real ownership of accessibility work.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names what else the title would need — actual authority to prioritise work and budget or headcount to act, not just the title itself.

hints: A title is one part of ownership. What else did lesson two say ownership actually requires?
explanation: False. A title is a real, positive signal, but it isn't sufficient on its own — the same gap applies if the title-holder has no budget, no authority to prioritise other teams' sprint capacity, and no measurable goals tied to remediation. A 'Head of Accessibility' with responsibility but no authority is a more official-sounding version of the unpaid Slack volunteer from lesson two: a name attached to the problem, without the power to move it.

prompt: Sort each scenario by which blocker it best illustrates.

items.text: Findings live only in a shared drive folder no tracker links to
"Accessibility" appears in the company values page; no team, budget or role is attached to it anywhere else
A 60-item remediation plan is reviewed once a quarter against a fixed 5% tech-debt slice and consistently loses to security work
A purchased certification badge appears on the homepage with no test report available from anyone at the company

hints: Ask what specifically is missing in each case: a path into the tracker, a named accountable role, a fair shot in a frequent comparison, or a real report behind a claim.
explanation: Each scenario isolates one blocker cleanly. Worth noticing: real stalled programmes are frequently a combination of two or more of these at once, which is exactly why the diagnosis in the lab asks you to name the primary one rather than list every plausible factor.

prompt: Match each intervention to the blocker it's actually designed to fix.

pairs.left: Filing findings as tickets directly in the team's own tracker
pairs.right: No routing

pairs.left: Naming a role with a measurable remediation goal and reserved sprint capacity
pairs.right: No real ownership

pairs.left: Sizing fixes in story points and entering them as ordinary backlog tickets
pairs.right: Losing to the roadmap

pairs.left: Asking whether a checkable test report exists before signing anything
pairs.right: Compliance theatre

hints: Each intervention in this module was designed as the specific answer to one specific blocker.
explanation: The four interventions map one-to-one to the four blockers this module covers — which is worth noticing precisely because a mismatched intervention (say, more training, aimed at a routing problem) can feel like progress while leaving the actual blocker untouched.

prompt: Put these diagnostic steps in the order you'd actually run them on a stalled programme.

items: Reconstruct what actually happened to the findings after delivery — who received them, what happened in the following meetings
Check whether the findings ever entered a system the team's real sprint planning reads from
If they did enter that system, check whether a named role with authority and reserved capacity exists to prioritise them
If ownership exists, check whether the fixes are competing as a separate programme or as ordinary sized tickets
Name the primary blocker and the specific intervention that addresses it

hints: This mirrors the order the module's four blockers were taught in, because each later check only makes sense once the earlier ones have passed.
explanation: Each check only makes sense once the one before it has passed — there's no point checking whether fixes compete fairly against the roadmap if they never had an owner to enter that competition in the first place, and no point checking ownership if the findings never even reached a system anyone could own.

prompt: A client says: "We did an audit two years ago, fixed maybe five things, and nothing's happened since — but everyone here genuinely cares about this." In three or four sentences, what would you actually ask them to figure out which blocker this is, before proposing anything?
hints: You have four candidate blockers from this module. What's the fastest question that would rule most of them out?
"Everyone cares" is compatible with all four blockers at once — it doesn't help you narrow anything down.
explanation: A strong answer asks specific, falsifiable questions rather than accepting the general 'everyone cares' framing: Where do the remaining findings from that audit currently live — in a tracker, or a drive folder? Is there a named person whose job includes this now? When it's come up in planning, what has it lost to? Each question is aimed at ruling in or out one specific blocker, which is the actual value of the diagnostic frame — 'people care' tells you nothing about which of the four mechanisms is actually stopping the work.

prompt: A proposal for a two-sprint remediation effort gets warm agreement from an engineering manager and a designer, in a meeting neither of them called. Three months on, nothing has moved. What's the most likely blocker?

options.text: Compliance theatre — the company never intended to act
The ask was never addressed to whoever actually controls the budget or roadmap capacity a two-sprint effort requires
No routing — the findings were never entered as tickets

hints: Warm agreement from people in a meeting isn't the same as agreement from whoever controls the resource being asked for.
explanation: The second option. Nothing in the scenario suggests theatre (there's no claim being made at all yet) or a routing failure (a proposal, not a stalled audit, is the object here) — what it does show is genuine enthusiasm from two people whose authority is real but narrower than the ask requires. A two-sprint effort is a roadmap and budget decision; neither an engineering manager nor a designer, however supportive, holds that specific resource on their own.

prompt: A team already runs a design review in Figma with comments before any code is written, every single time, without exception. Which of these is most likely to produce lasting accessibility attention with the least new overhead?

options.text: Proposing a separate, dedicated 'Accessibility Design Review' meeting after the regular one
Adding accessibility as one of the things reviewers are expected to comment on inside the design review that already happens
Waiting until after build and catching issues in QA instead, since design review is already busy enough
Sending a written accessibility guideline document to the design team to read on their own time

hints: The strongest option costs the team zero new calendar time.
A guideline document nobody is required to open at any specific moment tends to go unread — there's no existing step forcing anyone to look at it.
explanation: The second option. It attaches to a step that already happens, without exception, every single time — nothing new needs to be scheduled or remembered. A separate meeting adds calendar overhead that has to keep winning attention forever; catching issues in QA instead moves the check to the most expensive possible point, after the cost of building the wrong thing is already sunk; and an unread document has no existing moment forcing anyone to engage with it at all.

prompt: You're joining a team you don't know yet. In three or four sentences, describe how you'd spend your first week figuring out where to attach accessibility checking, before proposing anything at all.
hints: The goal of the first week is inventory, not intervention — find out what already happens without being reminded.
A good first question to ask several people: 'what's the one step nobody skips, no matter how busy things get?'
explanation: A strong answer describes observing or asking about the team's actual, existing rituals before suggesting anything new: which steps happen on every single change without exception (a PR template, a design review, a release checklist), who already looks closely at the work at each of those steps, and what a reviewer at that step already has authority to block or comment on. The point isn't to design the perfect intervention on day one — it's to avoid proposing a new ceremony before knowing whether a cheaper, already-existing one is sitting right there.

prompt: Sort each item by whether it's something you can meaningfully check directly in a static design file, or something that genuinely requires working code to test.

items.text: Whether text contrast against its background meets the required ratio
Whether the visual layer order matches a sensible reading and focus order
Whether a live region actually announces a dynamically updated element to a screen reader
Whether tap targets meet minimum size and spacing
Whether keyboard focus visibly moves to the right element after an action completes
Whether an error state is designed at all, or only the happy path

hints: Ask: can this be judged by looking at pixels and layers alone, or does it depend on runtime behaviour?
explanation: A design review reliably catches static, structural properties — contrast, implied order, target size, whether a state was designed at all. It cannot catch anything that only exists once code actually runs: live announcements, real focus movement, actual keyboard operability. Knowing this boundary is what keeps a design review honest about what it did and didn't cover, instead of quietly standing in for the code-stage review it can't replace.

prompt: A Figma frame shows a settings toggle where the only indication of on/off state is colour (green vs grey), with identical shape and no label change. Write the design-review comment you'd leave — specific enough that the designer could act on it without asking a follow-up question.
hints: Name the exact layer or component, state the actual problem, and suggest a concrete direction — not just 'this needs a fix.'
What would still communicate the state to someone who can't distinguish the two colours?
explanation: A workable comment names the component, states the problem in one sentence, and suggests a concrete fix direction: "Settings toggle (component: toggle-switch): on/off state is conveyed by colour alone (green/grey), with no shape or label change. Someone who can't distinguish the colours has no way to tell the state. Suggest adding a position change (circle moves left/right) and/or an 'On'/'Off' text label next to the toggle." This names the exact component, states the actual failure mode plainly, and gives the designer something concrete to try — not just an instruction to 'make it accessible.'

prompt: Put these steps of a pairing session that transfers real skill, not just a one-off fix, in order.

items: Reproduce the bug live, narrating exactly what you're doing
Ask the developer what they think the fix needs to do, before explaining anything
Explain the underlying mechanism, not just the specific line to change
Let the developer write the actual code change themselves
Retest together against the original expected behaviour

hints: This mirrors the same predict-before-explain order used everywhere else in the module — including how it teaches you.
explanation: Asking for a prediction only works before the explanation, not after — reversing steps two and three turns a genuine guess into a hollow one. And having the developer write the code has to come after the mechanism is understood, or it collapses into copying, which is exactly the 'fast but shallow' outcome the case study warns about.

prompt: True or false: taking over the keyboard and fixing a bug yourself while a developer watches is always the wrong choice during a pairing session.

config.statement: Taking over and fixing a bug yourself while a developer watches is always the wrong choice during a pairing session.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names the real trade-off — speed on this one fix versus the developer retaining and transferring the pattern — rather than treating it as a simple rule to always avoid.

hints: Think about genuine time pressure: a production incident, an urgent release. Is there ever a real reason to just fix it fast?
The lesson's case study calls this outcome 'mixed,' not 'costly' — that word choice is doing work.
explanation: False. Under real time pressure — a production incident, a release blocked on this one fix — taking over and moving fast can be the right call, and it's a legitimate trade-off, not a mistake. What the lesson argues against is defaulting to it as the normal way to pair, because it reliably produces a shallower kind of learning: the developer sees the fix once rather than reasoning through and writing it themselves, so the underlying pattern is less likely to transfer to the next similar bug. The skill is recognising which trade-off you're making and why, not treating 'let them write it' as an inflexible rule.

prompt: An audit turns up 25 findings of the same defect — a form field's error message isn't programmatically associated with its input — across 25 different forms, each built from the product's shared FormField component. How should this be reported?

options.text: 25 separate findings, one per form, since each affects a different page and user journey
One finding naming the shared root cause in the FormField component, listing all 25 affected instances, with the fix pointed at the component itself
One finding with no instance list, just a note that it's widespread

hints: The severity module covered exactly this shape of problem for a different reason — grouping by root cause, not by where each symptom happens to appear.
explanation: The second option. Filing 25 separate findings obscures that this is one fix, not 25, and risks 25 slightly different patches landing in 25 places instead of one correct fix at the source. A finding with no instance list loses the evidence a developer needs to confirm they've actually found the shared component and can verify the fix reaches every listed page. Naming the shared cause and listing every instance gives both the leverage and the evidence in one place.

prompt: True or false: once a defect is fixed and released in a shared component library, an auditor can mark every one of the original findings that trace to it as resolved.

config.statement: Once a defect is fixed and released in a shared component library, every original finding tracing to it can be marked resolved.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names the real gap — that each consuming surface has to actually adopt the new version before the fix reaches it — not just a general claim that 'you should double check.'

hints: A fix landing in a shared library's source code and a fix reaching a specific production page are two different, separately verifiable events.
explanation: False. A merged and released fix in the component library only reaches a given consumer once that team actually updates to the new version — some may be pinned to an older version for unrelated reasons, or simply haven't gotten to the update yet. The honest status per original finding is 'fixed at source, pending adoption' until each specific instance is retested and confirmed on the updated version, exactly the same discipline the retesting phase applied to any other fix.

prompt: A reviewer is praised as 'the person who catches everything' on their team. What question best tests whether the team has actually gained durable competence, versus just gained a dependency?

options.text: How many findings has this reviewer personally written in the past year?
If this person took a month of leave tomorrow, what would the team still be able to catch on their own?
How senior is this reviewer compared to the rest of the team?

hints: Resilience is measured by what survives the person's absence, not by how impressive their individual output is.
explanation: The second question is the real test. A high individual finding count or seniority level says something about current output, but nothing about what happens when that person is unavailable — which is precisely the axis 'dependency versus durable competence' is measured on.

prompt: Match each knowledge-transfer element to what it's actually meant to preserve.

pairs.left: A short decision log
pairs.right: The reasoning behind non-obvious calls that would otherwise only live in one person's head

pairs.left: A team-owned, team-edited checklist
pairs.right: Working knowledge that belongs to the team, not just knowledge the team consumes from one person

pairs.left: A second trained person running office hours
pairs.right: Redundancy that survives the primary reviewer being unavailable

pairs.left: Finding tickets in the tracker
pairs.right: Routine, specific defects — already covered without a separate log

hints: Ask what each artefact would still be true of if the original reviewer left tomorrow.
explanation: The four pieces target four different failure modes: lost reasoning, one-sided ownership, single points of failure, and (already solved) routine findings. Worth noticing that the fourth pairing is a reminder, not new information — routine findings don't need a separate log, because the tracker from module one already covers them.

prompt: A post-build finding reads: 'The date range picker has no visible focus indicator on its calendar cells.' What would the equivalent design-stage comment need to state, that a post-build finding doesn't have to?

options.text: Nothing extra — the same wording works at either stage
What the focus state should actually look like, since no focus state exists yet to point at and say 'this is missing'
The exact WCAG success criterion number

hints: At the design stage, there's no built focus behaviour yet to describe as broken — the comment has to specify what should be built.
explanation: A post-build finding can point at what's missing because something already exists to compare against. A design-stage comment has to be prescriptive rather than descriptive — it needs to specify what the focus state should look like (a border, an outline, a background change) since there's no existing behaviour yet to contrast it with. A citation can strengthen either version but doesn't solve this specific gap.

prompt: Sort each intervention by whether it rides an existing team process, or adds a new one.

items.text: A required accessibility checklist item added to the existing PR template
A brand-new weekly accessibility standing meeting
Comments left inside the design review that already happens before every build
A separate quarterly accessibility steering committee

hints: Ask whether the step already happens on every change, with or without accessibility in mind.
explanation: The pattern from lesson one, applied cold: anything attached to a step the team was already doing every time survives; anything requiring a brand-new, separately scheduled ritual has to keep winning attention against everything already on the calendar.

prompt: True or false: a design review can fully replace a code-stage accessibility review, since most of what matters is already visible in the design file.

config.statement: A design review can fully replace a code-stage accessibility review.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names at least one category of thing only checkable in working code — live announcements, actual keyboard operability, real focus movement — not just 'you should always double-check.'

hints: What kinds of properties genuinely can't be judged from a static file, no matter how carefully you look?
explanation: False. A design review reliably catches static, structural properties — contrast, implied order, target size, missing states — but cannot catch anything that only exists once code actually runs: whether a live region truly announces, whether focus genuinely moves where intended, whether a control is really keyboard-operable. Both stages are needed; each catches what the other structurally cannot.

prompt: Match each scenario to the strongest intervention from this module.

pairs.left: 18 findings across the product all trace to the same shared Card component
pairs.right: Fix at the component library level, then track adoption across consumers

pairs.left: A developer keeps making the same focus-management mistake in new components
pairs.right: Pair with them live on the next instance, explaining the mechanism

pairs.left: A reviewer is the only person on the team who can catch anything, and is about to go on leave
pairs.right: Build a decision log, a team-owned checklist, and train a second person

pairs.left: A contrast issue is caught the day before a feature ships to production
pairs.right: Fix it now, and separately push to get similar issues caught in design review earlier next time

hints: Each scenario names its own best-fit intervention from a different lesson in this module.
explanation: None of these interventions are interchangeable — a component-level problem needs a component-level fix, a recurring individual mistake needs pairing, and a single-point-of-failure risk needs redundancy, not another fix of any kind.

prompt: Put these steps of turning a post-build finding into a preventive design-review habit in order.

items: Notice the finding and identify what property of the design would have predicted it
Check whether the team already has a design-review step that happens on every change
Write the specific, measurable check that belongs in that step for this kind of issue
Propose adding it to the existing step, not a new one
Confirm on the next design file that the check actually gets applied

hints: This is lesson one's whole argument, run end to end on a single concrete finding.
explanation: Skipping straight to proposing a check without first identifying an existing step to attach it to is exactly how a well-intentioned fix turns into a new, fragile ceremony instead of a durable one.

prompt: You catch a missing-accessible-name defect on a shared icon-button component used in eight places. Write the one-paragraph message you'd send to the design-system team proposing the fix, including why it belongs there rather than on each of the eight pages.
hints: Name the component, the defect, the affected instances, and make the leverage argument explicit — one fix versus eight.
explanation: A strong message names the component and defect precisely, lists the eight known instances as evidence this is a shared-cause problem, and makes the leverage case directly: fixing it once in the design system reaches all eight now and every future use automatically, versus eight separate patches with eight chances to diverge. It should also flag, honestly, that each consuming team will still need to update their dependency before the fix reaches production — the trade-off lesson four's second half named.

prompt: A reviewer wants their eventual departure from a team to leave the least possible gap. Which of these does the least to actually reduce that risk?

options.text: Writing a decision log explaining the reasoning behind non-obvious calls
Personally reviewing every single PR themselves for as long as they're on the team, to keep quality high
Training a second person to run the accessibility office-hours slot

hints: Ask which of these three still leaves the team dependent on one person the day they leave.
explanation: Personally reviewing everything, however well done, is exactly the pattern that produces a bus factor of one — it maximises quality while that person is present and leaves nothing behind when they're not. The decision log and the trained second person are both explicitly aimed at reducing dependency, which is the actual risk being managed.

prompt: A contrast defect on a shared button component is found during a design review. The same defect, if it ships and is later flagged, would require finding every production instance, patching, retesting and releasing. Which framing of the cost most accurately reflects this situation?

options.text: Fixing it now costs roughly the same as fixing it after ship, so timing doesn't really matter here
Fixing it now, before build, is a small one-time cost; fixing it after ship compounds with every place the pattern was already reused
It should wait until after ship, since design-stage findings are usually not confirmed defects yet

hints: Think about what changes between 'a colour value in a file' and 'production code already shipped in several places.'
explanation: The second option. A design-stage catch is cheap precisely because nothing has been built yet to unwind — there's one value to change. A post-ship catch of the same defect on a shared, reused component means finding every instance, patching production code, retesting each, and releasing — and the count of places to fix only grows the longer the defect ships unnoticed.

prompt: You're about to pitch a remediation budget to a VP of Sales, whose role is measured almost entirely on closing enterprise deals. In two or three sentences, what's the strongest honest framing to lead with, and why?
hints: What do enterprise buyers, especially in the public sector or regulated industries, frequently ask about during procurement?
The framing has to be true, not just convenient — don't invent a claim you can't back up.
explanation: A strong answer leads with market reach translated specifically into what a Sales VP cares about: lost or stalled deals. For example — 'Several enterprise and public-sector buyers require an accessibility conformance statement during procurement; without one, or with one that doesn't hold up under scrutiny, deals in that segment either stall or lose to a competitor who can produce a real one. This is a revenue-blocking gap in the pipeline, not just a compliance nice-to-have.' This is true, specific to the sales role's actual incentives, and doesn't require inventing numbers the pitch can't back up.

prompt: True or false: a moving personal story about a disabled employee's resilience is always the wrong way to open a pitch for accessibility investment.

config.statement: A moving personal story about a disabled employee's resilience is always the wrong way to open a pitch for accessibility investment.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and identifies what actually matters — how the story is framed and where it ends, not whether a personal story is used at all.

hints: Is the problem the story itself, or specifically how it resolves?
explanation: False. A personal story can be a genuinely strong opener — vivid, concrete, hard to argue with. What determines whether it helps or backfires is the frame it's told in and where it lands: a version that resolves in praise for the person's resilience tends to produce admiration and no action, while the same true story, ending on the specific gap it reveals and the fix being proposed, gives the room something to actually decide on.

prompt:
Rewrite this pitch opener so it keeps every true fact but ends on a decision instead of an ovation:

"Despite using a screen reader, [NAME] manages to complete her expense reports every month — it's honestly inspiring to watch her persistence."
hints: What specifically makes the expense report process harder than it needs to be? Name the actual barrier.
End on the fix, not on the person's effort.
explanation: A strong rewrite keeps the true, specific fact but redirects the ending: "[NAME] completes her expense reports every month using a screen reader, despite the form's date picker and receipt-upload steps not being fully operable by keyboard — each report currently takes her roughly three times longer than it should. We're proposing to fix those two components this quarter, which would close that gap for her and for every other screen reader or keyboard user on the team." This keeps the individual's real experience as evidence, but ends on the specific fix and its scope — a decision the room can act on, not a compliment with nowhere to go.

prompt: Sort each opening statistic by whether it's defensible as the central number in a pitch to this specific product's stakeholders, or too broadly scoped to survive a follow-up question.

categories: Too broad — invites the follow-up question

items.text: "1 billion people worldwide live with some form of disability"
items.category: Too broad — invites the follow-up question

items.text: "Last quarter, 6% of our own support tickets referenced an accessibility barrier by name"
"Our own checkout funnel data shows a 40-point conversion gap for users flagged by our analytics as using assistive technology"
"Studies show accessible websites are generally better for everyone"
items.category: Too broad — invites the follow-up question

hints: Ask whether the number was measured on the actual product being pitched, or somewhere else entirely.
explanation: The defensible pair are both scoped to this product's own data. The other pair, though true and often cited, describe the world in general rather than this product specifically — exactly the gap a skeptical stakeholder's first question is likely to expose.

prompt: You genuinely don't know what share of your users would be affected by a specific barrier, and no data exists to find out cheaply. What's the strongest honest move in a pitch?

options.text: State a plausible-sounding estimate anyway, since a pitch with no numbers at all sounds weaker
Say plainly that the data doesn't exist yet, cite the nearest honest, named proxy if one exists, and propose the instrumentation to get a real number next time
Drop the quantitative argument entirely and rely only on the legal-risk framing instead

hints: An invented number and abandoning numbers altogether are both worse than naming the gap honestly and doing something about it.
explanation: The second option. An invented estimate is a liability the moment anyone asks where it came from, and dropping the quantitative case entirely gives up a genuinely useful lever without needing to. Naming the actual gap, citing an honest proxy if one exists, and proposing to close the gap as part of the ask turns a weakness into part of a credible, defensible plan.

prompt: True or false: writing a pitch email as if it might be forwarded with no added context is generally unnecessary, since the first recipient can always explain the background verbally.

config.statement: Writing a pitch email as if it might be forwarded with no added context is generally unnecessary, since the first recipient can always explain the background verbally.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and notes that the writer has no control over whether the first recipient actually adds context when forwarding — the message should carry its own context regardless.

hints: Who controls whether the first recipient adds context when they forward it — you, or them?
explanation: False. The original writer has no control over how the first recipient forwards the message — a busy engineering director is just as likely to forward it with a single line ('worth a look?') as with a full explanation. Since that's outside the writer's control, the safer and more reliable move is writing the message to carry its own context from the start, so it works whether or not anyone adds more.

prompt: Write the subject line and opening two sentences of a pitch email requesting budget to fix five Blocker-severity findings on a signup flow, written to survive being forwarded to someone who has never spoken to you.
hints: The subject line should name the actual topic and, ideally, the actual ask.
The first two sentences should work as a complete summary on their own — what's wrong, what's being asked.
explanation: A strong version: "Subject: Signup flow accessibility fixes — requesting sign-off on 1-sprint budget. Five Blocker-severity issues currently prevent screen reader and keyboard users from completing signup at all. Proposing roughly one sprint of engineering time to fix all five — details and evidence below." Both sentences work completely on their own for a reader with zero prior context: the topic, the scale of the problem, and the specific ask are all present before any further detail is needed.

prompt: A stakeholder responds to a personal-experience-only pitch with: "I'm sorry it's been hard for you, but I'm not sure how many other users this actually affects." What does this response reveal about how the case was built?

options.text: The stakeholder is simply being unreasonable and dismissive of disabled employees
The case had no evidence beyond one account to answer the prevalence question the stakeholder is now asking
The pitch should have been made to a different stakeholder entirely

hints: What could the presenter have pointed to, if the stakeholder's question had been anticipated?
explanation: The second option. The response is a predictable move available to any listener when personal testimony is the only evidence on offer — it's not really about whether the stakeholder cares, it's about what the case gave them to work with. A case with prevalence evidence alongside the personal account removes this specific opening.

prompt: Put these elements of a case that uses personal experience well in the order they should appear.

items: A short, vivid, specific personal account that makes the problem concrete
Evidence beyond that one account — usage data, other accounts, or an honestly labelled industry benchmark
A specific, sized ask addressed to whoever holds the relevant resource

hints: This mirrors the earlier module's ask-shaped ending, with a personal opening added in front of it.
explanation: The personal account earns attention and makes the problem concrete; the broader evidence answers the prevalence question the account alone can't; the sized ask gives the room something to actually decide on. Dropping or reordering any of the three reopens one of the gaps this module has named — an unanswerable prevalence question, or a case with no actionable ending.

prompt: A pitch to a chief financial officer opens with "accessibility is simply the right thing to do." What's the most useful next line to add, given who's in the room?

options.text: A longer explanation of why it's the right thing to do
A specific figure translating the ask into cost, risk or reach — the categories a CFO's role is actually measured against
Nothing — the moral case should be enough on its own

hints: What categories does a CFO's own job get measured in?
explanation: The second option. The moral opener isn't wrong, but a CFO's actual decision gets made in cost, risk and reach terms — the pitch needs to translate into at least one of those to become actionable for this specific audience, not just restate or extend the moral framing.

prompt: Sort each pitch fragment by which specific gap it has.

items.text: "It's amazing how [NAME] never lets his disability slow him down."
"Basically everyone agrees accessibility matters a lot."
"We really think leadership should take this more seriously going forward."
"1 in 4 adults has a disability, so obviously this is important for us too."

hints: Ask: does this resolve in praise, in an unscoped claim, or in nothing anyone can actually say yes to?
explanation: Each fragment fails in exactly one of the ways named across this module — an admiration-shaped ending, a number not scoped to the actual product, or a request too vague to be a real decision. Recognising which failure mode is in play is what determines the fix.

prompt: True or false: an email likely to be forwarded should save its most important information — the actual ask — for the end, so a busy reader has to read the whole thing.

config.statement: An email likely to be forwarded should save the actual ask for the end, so a busy reader has to read the whole thing to find it.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and explains that a forwarded message's real reader may only see the opening lines, so the summary and ask need to be upfront, not saved for a payoff at the end.

hints: What does a forwarded email's actual final reader typically see first, and how much of it do they reliably read?
explanation: False. A message likely to be forwarded needs its summary and its actual ask in the first two or three sentences, precisely because its real, final reader might only see the opening before deciding whether to keep reading, or might receive it with no further context at all. Saving the ask for a payoff at the end assumes a captive reader that a forwarded message often doesn't have.

prompt: Match each stakeholder to the framing most likely to land with them, based on what their role is actually measured against.

pairs.left: General counsel
pairs.right: Legal exposure and precedent from comparable cases

pairs.left: VP of Product
pairs.right: Market reach and conversion impact

pairs.left: Customer support lead
pairs.right: Specific, already-witnessed complaint patterns

pairs.left: A budget-holding VP with no prior context on the topic
pairs.right: A self-contained summary and a specific, sized ask up front

hints: The fourth pairing draws on the forwarding lesson, not the audience-matching lesson — the same underlying skill applied to a different problem.
explanation: The first three follow directly from matching an honest case to what a specific role is measured on. The fourth is the forwarding lesson's version of the same underlying skill — meeting the actual reader where they are, whether that's their role's incentives or their level of prior context.

prompt: Put these steps of handling a number you're genuinely unsure of, in a pitch, in the right order.

items: Resist the pull to state a precise-sounding number with no real source
State plainly what isn't known and why
Substitute the nearest honest, named, checkable proxy if one exists
Propose closing the gap as part of the ask itself

hints: This is lesson three's worked example, run end to end.
explanation: Each step depends on the one before it — you can't honestly substitute a proxy before first admitting the real number doesn't exist, and proposing to close the gap only makes sense once the gap itself has been named plainly.

prompt: A colleague drafts a pitch that opens: "As a wheelchair user myself, I can tell you firsthand how frustrating our office booking system is." and nothing else supports the case. In two or three sentences, what would you suggest adding, and why?
hints: The opening is genuinely strong. What's missing to keep it from being the entire case?
explanation: A strong suggestion keeps the personal opening (it's vivid and true) and adds what it can't provide alone: evidence beyond one person's account (usage or accessibility-request data, or an honestly labelled benchmark if none exists) that answers 'how many people does this actually affect,' plus a specific, sized ask to close on — so the case doesn't stand on one story alone and doesn't end without anything for a stakeholder to decide.

prompt: A pitch's opening line reads: "Following up as promised — here's the deck." What's the single biggest risk with this opening, specifically?

options.text: It's too casual in tone for a serious ask
It assumes shared context that its eventual, real reader — if forwarded — won't have, and names neither the topic nor the ask
It doesn't include a statistic

hints: What happens to this line if it's forwarded, with no note added, to someone who's never spoken to the sender?
explanation: The second option. Tone and the absence of a statistic are secondary issues; the disqualifying flaw is that the line carries zero standalone information — no topic, no ask — which means it fails completely the moment it reaches anyone outside the original conversation.
